Hello! Your tutorial certainly works for the most part. However, I have a few issues.

  • The code is lengthy for the task it addresses. Standing as a tutorial, much of the code is unexplained. Many of the definitions have redundant properties that can be minimized. There are eleven in your examples:

    • background-color
    • background-image
    • background-repeat
    • border-width
    • bottom
    • color
    • display
    • height
    • position
    • text-indent
    • width

    It is more efficient to apply these properties to the tabmenu li a node:

    .tabmenu li a,.tabmenu li.selected a {
 background: url([http://example.com/image.png](http://example.com/image.png)) no-repeat #222
 border: 0;
 bottom: -1px;
 color: #222
 display: inline-block;
 height: 25px;
 position: absolute;
 text-indent: -909px;
 width: 56px
}

    Then, apply unique properties if necessary:

    .tabmenu li:nth-child(1) a {
 left: 170px;
 /* other unique properties */
}

    Less bandwidth, faster loading, additional buffer room for additional styles and definitions, etc.

  • Images should not be used for the tabs. Not in the stictest sense, but the way it is applied in the tutorial is bad practice.

    Text should be displayed as much as possible for accessibility. Some users browse with images disabled and some others (visually impaired) rely on the text to navigate the site. I suggest removing the text-indent property and, instead, separate the tab background from the text.

    Also, a spritesheet* should be used for these purposes; both to save load time and clean up the code. With a spritesheet, we would first reference the image for all tabs:

    .tabmenu li a {background: url([http://example.com/image.png](http://example.com/image.png))}

    Then, adjust the positioning to select different images in the sheet for different tabs:

    .tabmenu li:nth-child(2) a {background-position: 0 -25px;}

  • Positioning. There are a few unnecessary properties being defined for the tabs that wouldn't suit WhoaVerse:

    • bottom
    • left
    • position

    The WhoaVerse stylesheet already defines the method of placement for the tabs and, to preserve compatibility, should be honored for the tab menu.

    One of the problems with absolute positioning is that it adds complication to scaling. As an example, when using media queries** to scale elements down when window widths decrease, additional properties need to be defined. If the tabs need to become smaller when the width decreases below a specific threshold...

    [@media](https://voat.co/u/media) (max-width: 500px) {
 .tabmenu li {font-size: 80%;}
}

    ...absolute positioning needs to redefined...

    [@media](https://voat.co/u/media) (max-width: 500px) {
 .tabmenu li {font-size: 80%;}
 .tabmenu li:nth-child(1) a {left: 150px;}
 .tabmenu li:nth-child(2) a {left: 200px;}
 /* ... */
}

    ...instead of just adjusting margins and padding...

    [@media](https://voat.co/u/media) (max-width: 500px) {
 .tabmenu li {
 font-size: 80%;
 margin: 2px; /* less than the default */
 padding: 2px; /* less than the default */
 }
}

    ...as it is defined by WhoaVerse's stylesheet.

As a tutorial, I suggest explaining why such code is being used and how it affects the elements so users know how to adjust it for their purposes. However, it depends on your audience.

Great tutorial nonetheless! I forgot that, using :nth:child()s, specific tabs could be styled; I thank you for that reminder! Have a nice day. :)

  1. CSS sprites are used in web design as a way to improve performance by combining numerous small images or icons into a larger image called a sprite sheet or tile set, and selecting which icon to show on the rendered page using Cascading Style Sheets. More on Wikipedia.
  2. A media query consists of a media type and at least one expression that limits the style sheets' scope by using media features, such as width, height, and color. More on Mozilla Developer Network.

Unfortunately, it's not the best option here because there's a simplier way to do it. Instead of using :afters, we can style the tabs with pure CSS without any gimmicks or images and keep the look. First, revert the tab styles.

Then, we'll cut the backgrounds out:

.tabmenu li a,.tabmenu li.selected a {
 background: none;
}

Next, the text colors:

.tabmenu li a,.tabmenu li.selected a {
 background: none;
 color: #DDD; /* Light gray text */
}

Make 'em all-caps:

.tabmenu li a,.tabmenu li.selected a {
 background: none;
 color: #DDD;
 font-family: Georgia,serif; /* Georgia font */
 text-transform: uppercase; /* All caps */
}

Style them a shiny, new border:

.tabmenu li a,.tabmenu li.selected a {
 background: none;
 border: 1px solid; /* Border */
 border-color: #555; /* Gray border */
 border-radius: 14px 14px 0 0; /* Curves top border corners */
 color: #DDD;
 font-family: Georgia,serif;
 text-transform: uppercase;
}

Breathing room:

.tabmenu li a,.tabmenu li.selected a {
 background: none;
 border: 1px solid;
 border-color: #555;
 border-radius: 14px 14px 0 0;
 color: #DDD;
 font-family: Georgia,serif;
 padding: 8px 12px 0; /* Breathing room */
 text-transform: uppercase;
}

Make Mr. Selected red to finish up:

.tabmenu li a,.tabmenu li.selected a {
 background: none;
 border: 1px solid;
 border-color: #555;
 border-radius: 14px 14px 0 0;
 color: #DDD;
 font-family: Georgia,serif;
 padding: 8px 12px 0;
 text-transform: uppercase;
}

.tabmenu li.selected a {
 border-color: #B22 #B22 #222;
 color: #B22;
}

With just 14 lines, we get this. Go ahead and tweak the colors and padding if necessary.
